lessonTitle: Arterial Supply of the Upper and Lower Limbs

blocks.text: A trauma patient arrives with a deep wound on the inside of the thigh and a cold, pulseless foot. To judge where the artery is injured, a doctor feels for pulses in a set order: groin, behind the knee, behind the ankle bone, and on top of the foot. Each pulse marks a point where the main arterial trunk runs close to the surface.

blocks.markdown: Each limb is supplied by a single long arterial trunk that changes name as it crosses landmarks. Learn the trunk, the points at which it renames itself, and the places where it can be felt. In the upper limb the trunk runs from the subclavian artery to the hand; in the lower limb from the external iliac artery to the foot. At joints the trunk is joined by **anastomoses** (connections between neighbouring branches), which provide collateral flow if the main vessel is blocked.

blocks.title: Arterial pathway: names change at landmarks
blocks.text: The same continuous vessel is given different names as it passes known landmarks. In the upper limb: subclavian artery, then axillary artery (from the outer border of the first rib), then brachial artery (from the lower border of teres major), then radial and ulnar arteries in the forearm. In the lower limb: external iliac artery, then femoral artery (below the inguinal ligament), then popliteal artery (after the adductor hiatus), then anterior and posterior tibial arteries.

rows: Arch of aorta on the left, brachiocephalic trunk on the right
Vertebral, thyrocervical trunk, internal thoracic; becomes axillary at the lateral border of the first rib
Lateral border of the first rib
Branches including the subscapular artery; becomes brachial at the lower border of teres major
Profunda brachii; ends in the cubital fossa by dividing into radial and ulnar arteries
Radial: mainly forms the deep palmar arch; ulnar: mainly forms the superficial palmar arch; common interosseous artery from the ulnar
Superficial arch gives common palmar digital arteries, which divide into proper palmar digital arteries to the fingers
blocks.caption: Arterial pathway of the upper limb from subclavian artery to digital arteries.

blocks.markdown: In the hand the **superficial palmar arch** (mainly from the ulnar artery) lies just under the palmar aponeurosis and gives off **common palmar digital arteries**, which divide into the **proper palmar digital arteries** supplying adjacent sides of the fingers. The **deep palmar arch** (mainly from the radial artery) lies deeper, on the bases of the metacarpals, and gives palmar metacarpal arteries. The two arches anastomose, so the hand survives loss of either the radial or the ulnar artery.

blocks.title: Tracing the upper limb pathway
blocks.prompt: Trace the path of blood from the subclavian artery to a fingertip.

steps.text: The subclavian artery passes over the first rib and continues as the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib.
The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major, and the brachial artery runs down the medial arm to the cubital fossa.
In the cubital fossa the brachial artery divides into the radial and ulnar arteries, which run down the forearm and form the palmar arches in the hand.
The superficial arch gives common palmar digital arteries, which divide into proper palmar digital arteries reaching the fingertip.

blocks.answer: Subclavian, axillary, brachial, radial and ulnar, palmar arches, common palmar digital, proper palmar digital arteries.

rows: Becomes the femoral artery at the inguinal ligament
Profunda femoris artery (deep artery of the thigh) arises in the femoral triangle; the main trunk passes through the adductor canal
Genicular branches; divides into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk
Passes through the interosseous membrane into the anterior compartment; becomes the dorsalis pedis artery at the ankle
Runs behind the medial malleolus and divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries; the fibular artery is the other branch of the trunk
blocks.caption: Arterial pathway of the lower limb from the external iliac artery to the foot.

blocks.title: Palpable pulses
blocks.text: Brachial: in the cubital fossa, medial to the biceps tendon (and in the medial arm), used for blood pressure measurement. Radial: at the wrist, just lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis. Femoral: at the midinguinal point, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis, below the inguinal ligament. Popliteal: deep in the popliteal fossa, felt with the knee flexed. Posterior tibial: behind and just below the medial malleolus. Dorsalis pedis: on the dorsum of the foot, lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus.

blocks.title: Locating the femoral pulse
blocks.prompt: A nurse needs to feel the femoral pulse. Where should she place her fingers, and what bony landmarks locate the position?

steps.text: Identify the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis.
The midpoint between them is the midinguinal point, which lies on the inguinal ligament.
The femoral artery passes under the inguinal ligament here, so palpate just below this point.

blocks.answer: Just below the midinguinal point, midway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis.

blocks.markdown: **Anastomoses and collateral supply.** Around the shoulder the scapular anastomosis links the subclavian artery with the axillary artery, providing a bypass if the axillary artery is blocked beyond the subscapular artery. Around the elbow, recurrent branches of the radial and ulnar arteries connect with branches of the brachial and profunda brachii arteries. In the lower limb, the cruciate and trochanteric anastomoses around the hip link the femoral and gluteal arteries, and genicular anastomoses around the knee connect the femoral, popliteal and tibial branches. These collateral channels help to preserve flow when a main trunk is narrowed.

items: Upper limb: subclavian, axillary, brachial, radial and ulnar, palmar arches, digital arteries.
Lower limb: external iliac, femoral, popliteal, anterior and posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis.
Arch pattern: superficial palmar arch mainly ulnar; deep palmar arch mainly radial.
Dorsalis pedis is the continuation of the anterior tibial artery.

blocks.title: Name changes occur at landmarks
blocks.text: The artery names change at fixed landmarks: first rib, teres major, inguinal ligament and adductor hiatus. If you can recall these four, you can name any segment of the trunk.

points: The upper-limb trunk is subclavian, axillary (from the first rib), brachial (from teres major), radial and ulnar, palmar arches, then digital arteries.
The lower-limb trunk is external iliac, femoral (from the inguinal ligament), popliteal (from the adductor hiatus), anterior and posterior tibial arteries, and dorsalis pedis.
Pulses can be felt at the brachial, radial, femoral, popliteal and posterior tibial sites, where the vessels lie superficially.

questions.stem: At which landmark does the axillary artery become the brachial artery?

options.text: Lateral border of the first rib

distractorRationale.b: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib.
distractorRationale.c: The brachial artery divides near the neck of the radius.
distractorRationale.d: This is not a landmark for renaming the artery.

questions.explanation: The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major. The brachial artery then runs down the arm to divide in the cubital fossa.

questions.stem: Where is the radial pulse best felt at the wrist?

options.text: Lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis
Medial to the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris

questions.correctOptionText: Lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis

distractorRationale.b: The ulnar artery is felt lateral to the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, not the radial.
distractorRationale.c: This is the site of the posterior tibial pulse.
distractorRationale.d: This is the site of the brachial pulse.

questions.explanation: The radial artery lies on the distal radius, just lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis, where it can be compressed against the bone. This is the usual site for counting the pulse.

questions.stem: The femoral pulse is felt at which site?

options.text: Midinguinal point, midway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis
Midway between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity
Behind the knee in the popliteal fossa
Over the dorsum of the foot

questions.correctOptionText: Midinguinal point, midway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis

distractorRationale.b: That is the approximate position of the sciatic nerve in the buttock.
distractorRationale.c: That is where the popliteal pulse is felt.
distractorRationale.d: That is where the dorsalis pedis pulse is felt.

questions.explanation: The femoral artery passes under the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point. It can be felt just below this point against the head of the femur.

questions.stem: The popliteal artery divides into which two branches?

options.text: Anterior tibial artery and tibioperoneal trunk

questions.correctOptionText: Anterior tibial artery and tibioperoneal trunk

distractorRationale.b: These arise from the brachial artery in the upper limb.
distractorRationale.c: The profunda femoris arises from the femoral artery in the thigh.
distractorRationale.d: These arise more distally from the tibial arteries.

questions.explanation: The popliteal artery divides into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk, the latter giving the posterior tibial and fibular arteries. The anterior tibial artery passes through the interosseous membrane to the anterior compartment.

questions.stem: Where is the posterior tibial pulse felt?

options.text: Behind and just below the medial malleolus
In front of the lateral malleolus
On the lateral side of the extensor hallucis longus tendon on the dorsum of the foot

questions.correctOptionText: Behind and just below the medial malleolus

distractorRationale.b: This is not a standard pulse point.
distractorRationale.c: This describes the dorsalis pedis pulse.
distractorRationale.d: The lateral side is where the fibular tendons run, not the posterior tibial artery.

questions.explanation: The posterior tibial artery runs behind the medial malleolus, between the tendon of flexor digitorum longus and the tibial nerve region, and can be felt there. It divides into the medial and lateral plantar arteries.

questions.stem: The dorsalis pedis artery is the continuation of which artery?

distractorRationale.b: The posterior tibial artery divides into the plantar arteries.
distractorRationale.c: The fibular artery supplies the lateral compartment.
distractorRationale.d: The popliteal artery divides above this level.

questions.explanation: The anterior tibial artery passes into the anterior compartment of the leg and becomes the dorsalis pedis artery at the ankle. Its pulse is felt lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus.

questions.stem: True or false: the superficial palmar arch is mainly formed by the radial artery.

distractorRationale.a: The superficial palmar arch is mainly from the ulnar artery; the deep arch is mainly from the radial artery.

questions.explanation: The superficial palmar arch is mainly a continuation of the ulnar artery and the deep palmar arch is mainly from the radial artery. The two arches anastomose, which protects the hand if one artery is blocked.

questions.stem: Which pulse is used for taking blood pressure with a cuff and stethoscope?

options.text: Brachial pulse in the cubital fossa

questions.correctOptionText: Brachial pulse in the cubital fossa

distractorRationale.b: The dorsalis pedis is on the foot.
distractorRationale.c: The popliteal pulse is behind the knee.
distractorRationale.d: The posterior tibial pulse is behind the medial malleolus.

questions.explanation: The brachial artery lies medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa, where the stethoscope is placed. The artery is easily compressed by the cuff.

questions.stem: Trace the arterial pathway from the subclavian artery to the digital arteries, naming the landmarks at which the vessel changes name.
markingGuide: Subclavian artery becomes axillary at the lateral border of the first rib.
Axillary becomes brachial at the lower border of teres major.
Brachial divides into radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa.
Ulnar artery mainly forms the superficial palmar arch; radial artery mainly forms the deep palmar arch.
Superficial arch gives common palmar digital arteries that divide into proper palmar digital arteries.
questions.explanation: The same continuous vessel has several names, so tracing it relies on knowing the landmarks. The palmar arches connect the radial and ulnar territories.

questions.stem: Trace the arterial pathway from the femoral artery to the dorsalis pedis and state where the femoral, popliteal and posterior tibial pulses are palpated.
markingGuide: Femoral artery gives the profunda femoris and passes through the adductor canal to the adductor hiatus.
Becomes the popliteal artery, which divides into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk.
Anterior tibial artery passes through the interosseous membrane, descends in the anterior compartment and becomes dorsalis pedis at the ankle.
Femoral pulse: below the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point.
Popliteal pulse: deep in the popliteal fossa with the knee flexed; posterior tibial pulse: behind the medial malleolus.
questions.explanation: The femoral, popliteal and tibial arteries form one continuous trunk. Palpating pulses in sequence helps to locate a blockage or injury.
